title: Public charitable trusts
summary: How a public charitable trust is established, who holds and manages its property, and the duties of trustees.

chunks.heading: What a trust is and how it is established
chunks.explanation_md:
A **trust** is a not-for-profit form that can be set up for **relief of poverty, education, medical relief, recreation facilities** and any other object of general public utility.

- **Public versus private**: public charitable trusts benefit members of an uncertain and fluctuating class. The key test is whether the class to be benefited is a **substantial segment of the public**.
- **Registration**: it must register with the **Charity Commissioner** of the state to be eligible to apply for tax-exemption.
- **Irrevocable**: Indian public trusts are generally irrevocable.
- **Law**: no national law governs public charitable trusts, though many states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and MP) have Public Trusts Acts.
- **Documents**: a trust of immovable property can be created by a non-testamentary document or a testamentary document such as a will. It **cannot be created orally**, only by a duly registered document.

key_terms.meaning: A trust for the benefit of the public, registered with the Charity Commissioner of the state, generally irrevocable.

chunks.exam_line: Trust: registered with the Charity Commissioner; generally irrevocable; immovable property trust needs a registered document, not oral.

chunks.heading: Trustees: who they are and what they cannot do
chunks.explanation_md:
- **Number**: at least **two trustees** are needed to register a public charitable trust.
- **Ownership**: legal title to the trust property **vests in the trustees**.
- **No private gain**: trustees may not use trust property or their position for their own interest or private advantage.
- **No conflicts**: they may not enter agreements in which they have a personal interest that conflicts, or may conflict, with the beneficiaries' interests.
- **Delegation**: they may not delegate duties, functions or powers to a co-trustee or anyone else, except **ministerial acts**. In essence, authority for duties needing discretion cannot be delegated.

key_terms.meaning: Holder of legal title to a public charitable trust property; may not use it for private advantage or delegate duties requiring discretion.

chunks.exam_line: Minimum two trustees; legal title vests in trustees; no private advantage, no conflicts of interest, no delegation except ministerial acts.

chunks.heading: Charity Commissioner oversight and cy-pres
chunks.explanation_md:
- In many states, a **purchase or sale of property by a trust** must be approved in advance by the Charity Commissioner.
- If a trust becomes **inactive through the trustees' negligence**, the Charity Commissioner may take steps to revive it.
- If it becomes too difficult to carry out the trust's objects, the **doctrine of cypres**, meaning "as near as possible", may be applied to change the objects.

key_terms.meaning: Meaning "as near as possible"; may be applied to change a trust's objects when carrying them out becomes too difficult.

chunks.exam_line: Charity Commissioner approves property deals, can revive an inactive trust; cypres changes objects "as near as possible".

questions.stem: Explain how a public charitable trust is established.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **public charitable trust** can be set up for relief of poverty, education, medical relief, recreation facilities or any object of general public utility, benefiting a substantial segment of the public.

- It must register with the **Charity Commissioner** of the state to be eligible to apply for tax-exemption.
- At least **two trustees** are required.
- A trust of immovable property needs a **registered document**; it cannot be created orally.
- Indian public trusts are generally irrevocable.

questions.stem: State the duties and limits on trustees.
questions.model_answer_md:
Trustees hold the legal title to trust property and must protect the beneficiaries' interests.

- They may not use trust property or their position for **private advantage**.
- They may not enter agreements where their personal interest conflicts with the beneficiaries' interests.
- They may not delegate duties, functions or powers, except **ministerial acts**; duties needing discretion cannot be delegated.

questions.stem: What powers does the Charity Commissioner have over a trust?
questions.model_answer_md:
The **Charity Commissioner** oversees trusts.

- In many states a trust's purchases or sales of property must be **approved in advance** by the Commissioner.
- If a trust becomes inactive through trustees' negligence, the Commissioner may take steps to **revive** it.

Separately, the doctrine of cypres lets a trust's objects be changed to something as near as possible when carrying them out becomes too difficult.

questions.stem: Explain the public charitable trust as a not-for-profit form: how it is established, who manages it and what rules bind its trustees.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **trust** is one of the three not-for-profit forms in Indian law, next to societies and Section 8 companies.

**Establishment.** It can be established for relief of poverty, education, medical relief, recreation facilities and other objects of general public utility. A **public** trust benefits an uncertain and fluctuating class, and the test is whether that class is a substantial segment of the public. It must register with the **Charity Commissioner** of the state to apply for tax-exemption. No national law governs it, though states such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and MP have Public Trusts Acts. A trust of immovable property needs a duly registered document and cannot be created orally; it may be by a will or non-testamentary document. Public trusts are generally irrevocable.

**Management.** At least **two trustees** are needed. Legal title to the property vests in the trustees; the trust is governed by its trustees.

**Rules for trustees.** They may not use property or position for private advantage, may not have conflicting personal interests, and may not delegate duties needing discretion, except ministerial acts.

**Oversight.** Many states require Charity Commissioner approval for property purchases or sales; the Commissioner may revive an inactive trust; the cypres doctrine can change objects as near as possible when they become too difficult.

In conclusion, a trust is a permanent, trustee-run structure that is tightly overseen.

questions.stem: Differentiate a trust from a society.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **trust** and a **society** are both not-for-profit forms, but they differ in structure.

| Basis | Trust | Society |
|---|---|---|
| Registration | Charity Commissioner of the state | State Registrar of Societies |
| Minimum people | At least two trustees | At least seven individuals |
| Governance | Governed by trustees | Governing council or managing committee elected by the members |
| Property | Legally vests in the trustees | Held in the name of the society |
| Annual filing | Not required to file the committee list | Files a list of managing committee members with the Register of Societies |
| Dissolution | Generally irrevocable | May be dissolved with approval of at least three-fifths of members |
| Law | State Public Trusts Acts in many states | Societies Registration Act 1860 |

On dissolution a society's remaining funds may not go to its members; they pass to another society, preferably with similar objects.

In conclusion, a trust is run by a few trustees who hold the property, while a society is a membership body run by an elected committee.
